title: Hyper-NA EUV: The Next Frontier in Chipmaking Could Arrive in 2036
gist: Hyper-NA EUV (numerical aperture of at least 0.75) could be ready around 2036 per ASML and Zeiss engineers, but ASML has not committed to producing it and no delivery date exists. The nearer milestone is High-NA, which TSMC plans to use in high-volume manufacturing in 2030.

insights.claim: Hyper-NA EUV could be ready around 2036, based on a roughly ten-year outlook from ASML and Zeiss engineers, but this is a development horizon and not a confirmed delivery date.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: Not a near-term revenue driver for ASML; treat 2036 as option value.
insights.quote: no firm shipment schedule has been announced

insights.claim: ASML has begun development of Hyper-NA but has not committed to producing the machine, and readiness, first customer delivery and widespread adoption may occur at different times.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: Production commitment depends on customer investment justification.

insights.claim: The nearer milestone is High-NA: ASML and TSMC plan for TSMC to use High-NA in high-volume manufacturing in 2030, alongside a larger-mask system readiness initiative targeting 2033.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: High-NA adoption timeline is the actionable catalyst for lithography suppliers.

insights.claim: ASML's 0.33-NA EUV resolves 13nm and 0.55-NA High-NA 8nm at the same 13.5nm wavelength; Hyper-NA keeps the wavelength and raises aperture to at least 0.75.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: Further scaling comes from optics, not shorter wavelength.

insights.claim: Moving from 0.55 NA to 0.75 NA implies about 27 percent smaller printable dimensions through aperture alone, though actual results depend on illumination, masks, materials and processing.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: Upper-bound illustration, not a guaranteed transistor size.

insights.claim: 0.75-NA single exposure could replace some multiple-patterning applications done on 0.55-NA tools, reducing complexity on selected layers, though overall cost depends on productivity, reliability and yield.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: Cost advantage is unproven; watch tool productivity.
insights.locator: The economic attraction extends beyond smaller features

insights.claim: Higher aperture reduces depth of focus, forcing tighter wafer flatness, focus control and thinner resist films while controlling defects and pattern variation.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: Resist and metrology suppliers face rising requirements as NA increases.
insights.quote: Higher aperture reduces depth of focus

insights.claim: Hyper-NA's benefits to users would appear only indirectly via future processors and memory, and also require advances in transistor architecture, interconnects and packaging.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: Lithography alone does not deliver scaling gains.
